Yongjia Collection on the Precepts against Lust” says: “(A woman’s beauty) corrupts virtue and obstructs the Way; the offense is most grave. One should keep far from it, as one would avoid an enemy. Therefore the wise regard it in the thought of a venomous snake, and would rather come near a venomous snake than be intimate with a woman’s beauty.”

blocks.text: Chapter 26. Mara Tempts the Buddha

inline.s: The heavenly beings offered celestial maidens to the Buddha, seeking to corrupt his mind of the Way. The Buddha said: “You are but skin-bags stuffed with filth. Why have you come here? Begone! I have no use for you.” The heavenly beings revered him the more, and asked him about the Way. The Buddha expounded it for them, and at once they attained the fruit of stream-entry.

The heavenly beings offered fairies to the Buddha, hoping to destroy his aspiration. The Buddha said to them: “You are nothing but foul leather bags crammed with impurities. Why have you come here? Be off at once — do not make me sick.” Thereupon the heavenly beings respected the Buddha even more, and begged him for the Dharma. The Buddha then explained it for them, and the heavenly beings realized the fruit of stream-entry.

blocks.text: Chapter 27. Non-Attachment Attains the Way

inline.s: The Buddha said: One who practices the Way is like a log in the river, borne along by the current. If it does not run aground on either bank, is not seized by men, is not hindered by ghosts and spirits, is not caught in a whirlpool, and does not rot, I guarantee it will reach the sea. The student of the Way who is not deluded by passion and desire, not harassed by the many false views, and presses on with diligence and without contrivance — I guarantee that such a one will surely attain the Way.

One who studies the Way is like a piece of wood floating in the river, drifting with the current. So long as it is not snagged on either bank, not carried off by someone, not blocked by ghosts and spirits, not held fast in a whirlpool, and does not rot, I assure you it will surely reach the sea. Likewise, a student of the Way, so long as he is not deluded by passion and desire, not disturbed by the many false views, and advances with vigor without contrived striving — I assure you that such a person will certainly attain the Way.
[xun] along; following.
[rao] to disturb; to harass.

blocks.text: Chapter 28. Do Not Give Rein to the Mind-Horse

inline.s: The Buddha said: Trust not your mind, for your mind is not to be trusted. Above all, beware of dalliance with the opposite sex, for such dalliance breeds calamity. Only when you have attained arhatship may you trust your own mind.

Above all, do not trust your own thoughts (the mind), for your thoughts cannot be trusted. Be most careful not to associate with the opposite sex, for such contact gives rise to misfortune. Only after attaining the fruit of arhatship may you trust your own mind.
[yi] the mind; that which the heart schemes and ponders.

The thoughts of an ordinary person are ever deluded and turned upside down — like a moth that hurls itself upon the flame. One pities it and drives it away, yet the instant one is heedless it flings itself back, until it is burnt to death. The moth dies not because of the fire but because of the error of its own mind. So too a person who meets the opposite sex and casts himself into the fire of ruin: the fault lies in himself, not in the thing. From beginningless eons, sentient beings have wandered in the round of birth and death solely because they indulged their passions and followed their thoughts. How great indeed is the harm that the mind does to us!

Only after attaining the fruit of arhatship may you trust your own mind.” For the arhat has already severed the delusion of false views and the delusion of false thought, so that he is no longer swayed by mistaken minds and habitual tendencies.

blocks.text: Chapter 29. Contemplating Sensuality Aright

inline.s: The Buddha said: Beware of gazing upon women, and do not converse with them. If you must speak with them, set your mind aright and reflect: “As a renunciant dwelling in this defiled world, I should be as a lotus, unstained by the mud.” Think of the aged as your mother, those a little older as your elder sister, those younger as your younger sister, and the young as your daughter. Rouse the mind that longs to free them, and let evil thoughts be extinguished.

Take the greatest care not to look at women, and do not speak with them. If circumstances oblige you to do so, compose your mind and think aright: “I am a renunciant dwelling now in a defiled age; I should be like the lotus, unstained by the mud.” For the aged, reflect: this is my mother; for those somewhat older, this is my elder sister; for those younger, my younger sister; for the young, my daughter. Thus a compassionate heart to carry them beyond this world is born, and with it evil thoughts are stilled.
This is the method of keeping far from women, guarding against transgression, nurturing goodness, and extinguishing evil.

blocks.text: Chapter 30. Fleeing the Fire of Desire

inline.s: The Buddha said: One who practices the Way is like a man wrapped in dry grass — when the fire comes, he must flee. A seeker, seeing desire, must always keep far from it.

One who studies the Way is like a man wrapped in dry grass; when the fire comes he must swiftly take refuge from it. So when a student of the Way sees the things that kindle desire within him, he should flee far away, as grass avoids fire.

Toward desire, the student of the Way should practice the virtue of withdrawal, and never let himself be burned by the fire of craving. The Sutra of Perfect Enlightenment says: “To know the illusory is at once to be released from it, with no need of expedient means; released from the illusory, at once you are awakened, with no gradual stages.”

blocks.text: Chapter 31. When the Mind Is Still, Desire Is Eradicated

inline.s: The Buddha said: There was a man distressed by unceasing lust who wished to sever his own organ. The Buddha told him: Better than cutting away the organ is cutting away the mind. The mind is the magistrate; if the magistrate comes to rest, all his attendants are still. If the evil mind does not cease, what is the good of severing the organ? The Buddha then spoke this gatha for him: Desire is born within the mind, and mind of thought is wrought; when both are still and left behind, no form, no act is brought. The Buddha said: This gatha was spoken by the Buddha Kashyapa.

There was a man who gave way to lust and could not stop, and wished to cut away his own organ. The Buddha said to him: Far better than cutting away the organ is cutting away the mind. The mind is the magistrate; if the magistrate commands a halt, all his underlings come to rest as well. If the evil mind does not cease, of what use is cutting away the organ? The Buddha spoke this gatha for him: Desire is born within the mind, and mind of thought is wrought; when both are still and left behind, no form, no act is brought. The Buddha said: This gatha was spoken by the Buddha Kashyapa.
This is to say: to cut off desire, one must cut it off from the mind.

[gongcao] An official title. In the Han dynasty a commandery governor kept a recorder of merit (gongcao shi), shortened to gongcao, who, besides handling personnel, could take part in the administration of the whole commandery. [sixiang] Si and xiang. Here si (sī) means longing or remembrance, and xiang (xiǎng) means wishing or wanting. [Neither form nor act] When the two minds are each at rest, one awakens to the truth that sensual forms and evil conduct are both illusions; this is spoken with regard to the real nature of all dharmas.

blocks.text: Chapter 32. Severing Desire and Casting Off Attachment

inline.s: The Buddha said: From love and desire arise anxiety, and from anxiety arise fear. If one is free of love, what anxiety is there? What fear?
Because of love and desire, people give rise to anxiety; from anxiety they give rise to fear. If one abandons love and desire, what anxiety is there? What fear?
Therefore, to escape the restless unease within, one must sever desire and cast off attachment.

blocks.text: Chapter 33. Vanquishing Mara and Attaining the Way

inline.s: The Buddha said: One who practices the Way is like a single man at war with ten thousand. Donning his armor and going out from the gate, his will is sometimes faint; some turn back halfway, some fall in battle, some return in victory. So the renunciant who studies the Way should hold his mind firm, advance with diligence and valor, fear no prospect before him, destroy the many demons, and so attain the fruit of the Way.

One who studies the Way is like a single man joining battle with ten thousand. In war the warrior buckles on his armor and goes out from the city gate to meet the foe — or his will is faint, or he retreats halfway, or he dies fighting, or he returns in triumph. So too the renunciant’s study of the Way is like going to war: he should hold his mind firm (not be faint of will), press forward with diligence and valor (not retreat halfway), have no dread of what lies ahead (setting aside life and death), destroy the many demons, and so attain the fruit of the Way (return in triumph).

The liturgy of the Threefold Contemplation by Master Zhongfeng says: “All suffering is born of greed and craving, yet who can say where greed and craving rise? Because one forgets the Amitābha of one’s own nature, and all the scattered, racing thoughts are Mara’s work.”

blocks.text: Chapter 34. Attaining the Way by the Middle Course

inline.s: A renunciant was reciting at night the Bequeathed Teachings of the Buddha Kashyapa, his voice mournful and strained, and he began to think of retreating from the path. The Buddha asked him: When you dwelt at home, what was your occupation? He replied: I loved to play the lute. The Buddha asked: If the strings are too loose, how is it? He replied: They give forth no sound. The Buddha asked: If too taut? He replied: The note breaks off. The Buddha asked: If, neither loose nor taut, the strings are tuned aright? He replied: Then all the notes are harmonious. The Buddha said: Even so is the renunciant who studies the Way — if the mind is tuned aright, the Way is attained. If one is violent in the Way, violence wearies the body; when the body is weary, the mind grows vexed; when the mind is vexed, the practice recedes; and when the practice recedes, guilt increases all the more. Only in purity and serene ease is the Way not lost.

A renunciant recited at night the Bequeathed Teachings of the Buddha Kashyapa, his voice mournful and strained, feeling that the study of the Way was too hard and too wearying, and wishing to give up. The Buddha asked him: When you were at home, what was your trade? He answered: I loved to play the lute; playing the lute was my trade. The Buddha asked: If the strings are loosened too far, what happens? He answered: No note comes forth. The Buddha asked: If they are drawn too tight? He answered: They snap at a touch. The Buddha asked: If they are tuned just right, loose and tight in measure? He answered: Every note is true and sweet. The Buddha then taught: Studying the Way is like this — if body and mind are tuned aright, in just proportion, then as you practice you may attain the Way. If you are too fierce and urgent, then a person grows weary; weary, the mind grows vexed; vexed, you think of retreating and giving up; and once you give up, guilt and evil accumulate until you fall. Only by tuning body and mind aright, in purity and ease, can you advance steadily, practice long and with effect, and so never turn back.
[Buddha Kashyapa] The Buddha who came before Śākyamuni Buddha.

Confucius, too, had a word on tension and relaxation, saying: “To be always strained and never relaxed — even Kings Wen and Wu of the Zhou could not sustain it; to be always relaxed and never strained — that is something Kings Wen and Wu would never do. Let tension and relaxation alternate, and that is the way of Wen and Wu.”

This passage means: to keep straining without ever relaxing is beyond the power even of King Wen and King Wu, who governed the realm so well; and conversely, to remain forever at ease without ever straining is something Wen and Wu would never consent to. Only by joining labor and rest, severity and leniency, so that work and life move forward in their proper rhythm — this is how King Wen and King Wu governed the land.
Therefore the practice of the Way should be continuous and unbroken — water dripping slowly wears through stone.

blocks.text: Chapter 35. When the Defilements Are Cleansed, the Brightness Remains

inline.s: The Buddha said: Just as a man forges iron and, casting off the dross, makes a vessel, so the vessel at last proves fine and excellent — in the same way one who studies the Way, by removing the defilements of the heart, becomes pure in conduct.

Just as by forging iron into a vessel — hammering out the dross within — the vessel becomes fine and durable, so the student of the Way, by removing the defilements of the heart, becomes pure in conduct.
Therefore, practice is the cultivating of the mind: remove the heart’s defilements.

[Just as a man forges iron, casting off dross to make a vessel] Today steelmaking removes the impurities from molten iron by chemical means to obtain steel, which is then forged into tools. In ancient times the iron was heated red-hot and hammered again and again, each time driving out the dross, until steel was won — the proverb “a hundred refinements make steel.” For tools and weapons, steel is far sharper and more lasting than iron. Hence in olden days, to forge a vessel meant not only beating it into the desired shape but, in the very process, casting out the dross within — what is called “casting off the dross to make a vessel.”

blocks.text: Chapter 36. Winning the Goal Through Every Hardship

inline.s: The Buddha said: Having escaped the evil destinies, it is hard to be born a human. Becoming a human, it is hard to be born a man and not a woman. Being born a man, it is hard to be born with the six faculties whole. With the six faculties whole, it is hard to be born in the central kingdom. Born in the central kingdom, it is hard to meet a Buddha in the world. Meeting a Buddha, it is hard to encounter one who walks the Way. Encountering such a one, it is hard to arouse a heart of faith. Having aroused faith, it is hard to set forth the bodhi mind. Having set forth the bodhi mind, it is hard to be without practice and without attainment.

It is hard, having left the three evil destinies, to be born a human. Born a human, it is hard to be a man and not a woman. Born a man, it is hard to have the six faculties whole. Having the six faculties, it is hard to be born in the central kingdom. Born in the central kingdom, it is hard to meet a Buddha alive in the world. Meeting a Buddha, it is hard to encounter the Dharma. Encountering the Dharma, it is hard to arouse a heart of faith. Having aroused faith, it is hard to develop the aspiration to enlightenment. Having developed the bodhisattva resolve (the bodhi mind), it is hard to be without practice and without attainment.

[Three evil destinies] The hells, the realm of hungry ghosts, the animal world. [Six faculties whole] The six faculties are the eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind. To be whole in the six faculties means to lack the defects of blindness, deafness, dumbness, and maimed limbs. [Central kingdom] The “central kingdom” of ancient India, lying in the middle reaches of the Ganges, the heart of its civilization. [Bodhi mind] The resolve to attain Buddhahood above and deliver sentient beings below. [Without practice and without attainment] What was described earlier: the one ultimate vehicle, the most consummate path. [One vehicle] The way to Buddhahood.

This chapter means: good conditions are met by the student of the Way only after a hundred hardships and a thousand trials; and now, having struggled through to the step of setting forth the bodhisattva resolve, he should cultivate the most ultimate path.

blocks.text: Chapter 37. Keeping the Precepts Draws One Near the Way

inline.s: The Buddha said: Though a disciple be thousands of miles from me, if he keeps my precepts in mind, he shall surely attain the fruit of the Way. One who stands at my side, though he see me every day, if he does not follow my precepts, shall never attain the Way.

Though a disciple of the Buddha be thousands of miles from me, if he bears my precepts in mind, he shall surely attain the fruit of the Way. One who is at my side, though he sees me constantly, if he does not keep my precepts, shall never attain the Way.

Even to wait upon the Buddha on his left and right, without strictly keeping the precepts, one still cannot attain the Way — how much the more so in this latter age of the Dharma. From this we may know how essential it is to observe the precepts with strict severity.

blocks.text: Chapter 38. Human Life Is Impermanent

inline.s: The Buddha asked a renunciant: In how many intervals does a human life consist? He answered: Within a few days. The Buddha said: You do not yet know the Way. He asked another renunciant: In how many intervals does a human life consist? He answered: Within the space of a single meal. The Buddha said: You do not yet know the Way. He asked a third: In how many intervals does a human life consist? He answered: Within a single breath. The Buddha praised him: Well said — now you know the Way!

The Buddha asked one renunciant: In how many intervals does a human life consist? He answered: Within a few days. The Buddha said: You have not yet understood the Way. He asked another: In how many intervals does a human life consist? He answered: Within the space of one meal. The Buddha said: You have not yet understood the Way. He asked yet another: In how many intervals does a human life consist? He answered: Within one breath. The Buddha praised him: Excellent — now you understand the Way!
[Within a single breath] In the space of one in-and-out breath life may come to an end — what is meant by “the out-breath does not guarantee the in-breath.”

This chapter makes it clear: human life is impermanent, the out-breath does not guarantee the in-breath, and so the student of the Way must be alert and diligent, completing his task before death arrives.

blocks.text: Chapter 39. Sweet in the Midst and Sweet at the Edge

inline.s: The Buddha said: Those who study the Buddha’s Way should believe and follow all that the Buddha has spoken. It is like tasting honey — sweet in the midst and sweet at the edge; such likewise are my scriptures.

One who studies the Buddha’s Way should believe and follow everything the Buddha has spoken. As with the taste of honey, sweet at the heart and sweet at the rim, so too are the scriptures I have spoken.

Here the Buddha admonishes with heartfelt earnestness: those who study the Buddha’s Way should believe and follow all the Buddha’s words. Now there are those who, clinging to the small (the Hinayana), slander the great (the Mahayana), or clinging to the great, slander the small; those who cling to phenomena and reject principle, or cling to principle and reject phenomena — all of these run against the Buddha’s intent.

It is like studying mathematics. Someone judges arithmetic too elementary and would go straight to algebra; another finds algebra not lofty enough and would leap straight to calculus. And what is the result? After great effort they memorize a handful of terms and formulas from algebra or calculus and grow pleased with themselves, saying “I know algebra, I know calculus.” But can they solve a single problem with it? Since they cannot, of what use is their learning?

Studying the Buddha’s Dharma means subduing afflictions, severing afflictions, breaking through ignorance piece by piece, and realizing the fruit of Buddhahood in its fullness, so as to be done with the two deaths (the death born of segments and the death born of transformation). The Buddha’s teachings are set down for this very end. “Medicine is neither dear nor common; what suits the ailment is good. The Dharma is neither high nor low; what suits the capacity is excellent.” Therefore the student of the Way must take the medicine that suits his ailment, and learn so as to put it to use. If your own afflictions are not yet subdued, not yet cut off, and yet you scoff at the Buddha’s repeated admonition to “sever desire and cast off attachment” as mere Hinayana, refusing even to consider it, while you prattle on about the nature and the principle — is this not like one who, never having studied arithmetic or algebra, would go straight to calculus? When the last day of the twelfth month — the day of reckoning — arrives, will such learning stand you in good stead?

[Death born of segments] Among sentient beings within the three realms and six paths, because of the retribution of good and evil karma, the lifespan has its fixed limits and the body its divisions; hence their birth and death is called “death born of segments.” One who is done with this death is freed from the wheel of rebirth and passes beyond the three realms. [Death born of transformation] The noble ones of the three vehicles, having already severed the delusions of views and of thought and passed beyond the death of segments, find in the course of practice that delusive thoughts gradually die away and realization gradually grows. This shifting of delusion and awakening differs at each stage; the passage from one stage into the next is like a death, and the change is subtle, mysterious, and inconceivable — whence the name “death born of transformation.” One who is done with this realizes the fruit of Buddhahood in its fullness. [Three vehicles] The vehicle of the Hearer (Shravaka), the vehicle of the Solitary Realizer (Pratyekabuddha), and the vehicle of the Bodhisattva.

blocks.text: Chapter 40. Practicing the Way Lies in the Mind

inline.s: The Buddha said: In walking the Way, a renunciant should not be like the ox at the mill — though the body plods the path, the mind within does not. If the mind walks the Way, what need is there to move the body?
A renunciant walking the Way should not be like the ox that turns the mill: though the body treads the path, the mind has not. If the mind walks the Way, what need is there for the body to walk it?
Therefore, in practice the precious thing is to cultivate the mind; walking the Way lies in the mind, not in the outward form.

If the mind walks the Way, what need to move the body?” This is spoken for those who are “without thought, without abiding, without practice, without attainment.” If one has not yet reached the emptiness of both mind and states, then let the practice of the mind take the lead, body and mind advancing together. To take the correcting of faults as an example: there is correction by affairs, correction by principle, and correction by mind. On the relation and use of these three, Liao-Fan’s Four Lessons says: “On the whole, what is most excellent corrects the mind, and purity arises on the spot; the moment a thought stirs it is perceived, and being perceived it vanishes. If one cannot yet do this, one must comprehend principle so as to dispel it; and if still one cannot, one must restrain it together with the affair at hand. To practice the higher work while still carrying out the lower is no strategy at fault; but to cling to the lower and be blind to the higher is clumsy indeed.”

blocks.text: Chapter 41. An Upright Mind Escapes Desire

inline.s: The Buddha said: One who practices the Way is like an ox laden with a heavy load, trudging through deep mire — utterly spent, not daring to glance left or right, until he comes out of the mud and may at last rest. So too a renunciant should see that passion and desire are more perilous than mud, and, with an upright mind, think only of the Way, and so be free of suffering.

The practicer of the Way is like an ox burdened and walking through deep mud: though utterly exhausted, he dares not relax in the least — he will not even glance left or right until he has left the mire, and only then may he stop and take his rest. A renunciant should see that the peril of passion and desire is greater than that of mud, and only by fixing his whole mind on the Way, his eyes never turning aside, going bravely forward, can he emerge from desire and so be freed from suffering!
[suxi] To rest; to stop and catch one’s breath.

blocks.text: Chapter 42. All Dharmas Are Like an Illusion

inline.s: The Buddha said: I look upon the throne of kings and princes as upon grains of dust through a crevice. I look upon treasures of gold and jade as upon broken tiles. I look upon robes of finest white silk as upon tattered cloth. I look upon the great thousand-world as upon a single myrobalan. I look upon the waters of Lake Anavatapta as upon the oil used to anoint the feet. I look upon the gates of expedient means as upon a heap of conjured jewels. I look upon the supreme vehicle as upon gold and silk in a dream. I look upon the Way of the Buddha as upon flowers before the eyes. I look upon meditative absorption as upon Mount Sumeru standing firm. I look upon nirvāṇa as upon awaking from a day-and-night slumber. I look upon the inverted and the upright as upon the dance of six dragons. I look upon equality as upon the one true ground. I look upon the flourishing guidance of beings as upon the trees of the four seasons.

I regard the rank of kings and princes as dust drifting through a crevice. I regard the treasures of gold and jade as broken tiles. I regard robes of pure white silk as rotten rags. I regard the great thousand-world as a single myrobalan (the chebula fruit, wrinkled like an olive). I regard the waters of Lake Anavatapta as the oil for anointing the feet. I regard the many gates of expedient means as a heap of conjured jewels. I regard the supreme vehicle as the gold and silver of a dream. I regard the Way of the Buddha as empty flowers before the eyes. I regard meditative absorption as Mount Sumeru, towering immovably. I regard nirvāṇa as a man awaking from sleep. I regard the inverted and the upright as the dance of six dragons (a figure for the six faculties), head and tail merely exchanging place. I regard equality as the real ground of the one true realm. I regard the flourishing guidance of beings by the Dharma as the trees of the four seasons: budding in spring, luxuriant in summer, bearing fruit in autumn, dropping leaves in winter, in endless cycle.
Set at the close of the sutra, this chapter reveals the Buddha’s eye of equality beholding all things alike, in order to destroy beings’ clinging to dharmas.

[Clinging to dharmas] To cling wrongly to dharmas as real. The Buddha says: “Know that all dharmas are empty, illusory and without reality, having no root.” (The Sutra of Sustaining the World) [Dust through a crevice] Dust passing through a narrow crack — a figure for what is utterly trifling and fleeting, like a mote drifting before a tiny opening. [Broken tiles] Fragments of brick and stone. [Fine white silk] Exquisite, spotless white silk. [Tattered cloth] Worn-out, torn rags.

[Great thousand-world] That is, the great chiliocosm. One great thousand-world is the region in which a single Buddha teaches. Mount Sumeru together with the four great continents forms one small world; a thousand such small worlds form one small thousand-world; a thousand small thousand-worlds form one middle thousand-world; a thousand middle thousand-worlds form one great thousand-world. Since it is counted in thousands three times over, one great thousand-world is also called the “three-thousand great thousand-world.” [Mount Sumeru] Rendered in Chinese as “the lofty and wonderful mountain”; it is the center of one small world. This mountain is made of the four jewels — gold, silver, lapis lazuli, and crystal. Its form is broad above and broad below but narrow in the middle, exceeding tall and exceeding great, beyond comparison with any other mountain, the king of mountains. [Four great continents] About Mount Sumeru lie four great continents: in the east, East Videha; in the south, Jambudvipa (the world in which we dwell is on this continent); in the west, Godaniya; in the north, Uttarakuru. [Myrobalan] That is, the chebula fruit. The Compendium of Materia Medica says: “The Terminalia chebula tree is like the cork-tree; its flowers are white, its fruit like gardenia. Chiefly it disperses phlegm and sends the qi downward. It arrives on ships from beyond the southern seas, and is also found in Guangzhou.”

[Regarding the waters of Lake Anavatapta as like the oil for anointing the feet] To regard the dear waters of Lake Anavatapta as the cheap oil with which one anoints the feet — between them no difference at all. [Lake Anavatapta] That is, Lake Anavatapta, called “the lake without heat and vexation,” some eight hundred li in circuit. Its banks are adorned with the four jewels — gold, silver, lapis lazuli, and “beautiful crystal” (answering to this world’s crystal, which bears the four tints of purple, white, red, and green). Its bed is spread with golden sand, and its clear waves mirror like burnished glass. [Regarding the supreme vehicle as like the gold and silk of a dream] To regard the supreme vehicle as but the gold and silk seen in a dream. [Gold and silk] Gold and fine silk — in general, money and precious things. [Supreme vehicle] The Dharma of the utmost preeminence. Master Ouyi says: “Though the supreme vehicle is said to be the most real, yet it is all the principle inherent in the nature of sentient beings; outside the mind there is no Dharma. Hence it is said: perfect enlightenment returns to having nothing attained. Like the gold and silk of a dream — how could any real thing be gotten from it?”

[Regarding the Way of the Buddha as like flowers before the eyes] The many forms of the Buddha’s Way are set up to counter the deluded mind; if the deluded mind does not arise, how can there be any Way of the Buddha? The saying runs: “Unconditioned, neither arising nor ceasing, unreal as flowers in the sky.” [Flowers in the sky] Flowers in the open sky (the ancient word for blossom being the same as that for flower); a figure for illusion. One with a diseased eye sees flowers in the sky, yet in the sky there are no flowers at all — only the wrong perception of a diseased eye. The Sutra of Perfect Enlightenment says: “Mistakenly taking the four elements for one’s own body and the reflected images of the six dusts for the mark of one’s own mind — like the diseased eye seeing flowers in the sky and a second moon.”

[Regarding meditative absorption as like the pillar of Sumeru] Sumeru rises from the sea and wind and wave cannot move it; so too absorption holds the mind, and states and perceptions cannot sway it. Yet Sumeru is illusory, and absorption is illusory as well. [Pillar of Sumeru] That is, Mount Sumeru; the word “pillar” describes that mountain’s immeasurable mass, answering to the earlier “I look upon the great thousand-world as a single myrobalan.” [Regarding nirvāṇa as like awaking from a day-and-night slumber] Birth and death are as a long night, bound by ignorance, so by day and by night all are asleep; nirvāṇa is as the everlasting day, with wisdom opened wide, so by day and by night all are awake. [Regarding the inverted and the upright as like the dance of six dragons] In wheeling through birth and death there is only the six faculties; in the peace of nirvāṇa there is also only the six faculties. To turn away from enlightenment and mingle with the dusts is called “inverted,” yet in truth there is no decrease; to turn away from the dusts and join with enlightenment is called “upright,” yet in truth there is no increase. Hence it is but like the dance of six dragons (a figure for the six faculties), head and tail merely exchanging places — nothing more.

[Regarding equality as like the one true ground] To regard all dharmas as equal is like the one true ground. [One true ground] The real ground realized in the awakening to the one true realm. [One true realm] The single real dharma-realm, the only true realm — that is, the realm of the Buddha. The dharmakaya, equal for all Buddhas, from the very beginning neither arising nor ceasing, neither existing nor empty, beyond name and beyond mark, without within and without without, solely real and inconceivable — this is called “the one true realm.”
